G3373.portee: This parable invites the reader to understand that God's work in the human heart — as in the world — follows a silent and sure growth. We do not produce this growth by our efforts; we see it unfold, and one day it reaches maturity. It is a word of confidence: the Kingdom grows, no matter how it seems.

sens: rudimentary clothing made from a sheepskin or goat skin
garment of the poor or marginalized
G3374.detail:
1. A sheepskin is an animal hide, raw or simply tanned, worn as clothing. It is a minimal garment, unrefined, worn by those who have nothing else: in Hebrews 11:37, the heroes of faith persecuted "went about in sheepskins and goatskins."
2. This garment is the image of poverty and marginality: those who wear it are rejected, stripped, without resources. It is the visible sign of one who has lost everything for their faith.
G3374.origine: The Greek word comes from the ancient Greek *mêlon*, which means "sheep" or "goat." In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew *adéret*, the mantle or robe. Here, it specifically designates an animal hide, probably a raw skin wrapped around the body — the clothing of voluntary or forced destitution.
G3374.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:37. It is part of a list of the sufferings endured by the righteous of the Old Testament: stoning, saw, sword, but also this miserable exile clothed in skins. It is a concrete detail, a trait of biblical reality, showing that faithfulness to God can lead to total destitution.
G3374.portee: This word reminds the reader that the cost of faith can be extreme: not only death, but life reduced to the simplest survival, wandering, persecuted, without a home. It helps to measure the sacrifice of those spoken of in the letter to the Hebrews and to strengthen those who suffer for the Gospel.

sens: Particle that strongly affirms what precedes or follows
Mark of absolute certainty, of a solemn promise
G3375.detail:
1. This small Greek word does not have a direct equivalent in French, but it functions as a marker of assurance: it reinforces the statement and tells the reader "what follows is true, it is certain." In Hebrews 6:14, when God says "certainly I will bless you," this word removes all doubt: the blessing is guaranteed, it will truly come.
2. More specifically, when it introduces a promise (as is the case here with the promise made to Abraham), it underscores the solemnity of the oath and its irrevocable nature. God does not just say "I will bless you"; He swears: "certainly I will bless you," which elevates the word to an absolute divine commitment.
G3375.origine: This word comes from the common Greek language, where it appears in oaths and solemn affirmations. It is a very ancient particle that already appears in classical Greek poetry. In the Greek Bible (the Septuagint), it often translates Hebrew particles that mark the reinforcement of the oath, notably in formulas like "if... certainly." It is a word of guarantee and seriousness.
G3375.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 6:14, where it introduces the citation of a promise from God to Abraham taken from Genesis. The author of the epistle uses it to remind readers that divine promises are absolute and irrevocable. Its unique use shows that it is a solemn term, reserved for moments when it is necessary to affirm the unshakeability of God's word.
G3375.portee: For the Christian reading this epistle, this small word is an invitation to trust. When God says "certainly," He does not promise a mere possibility, but a reality. It teaches us that God's promises are not pious wishes, but commitments that will be fulfilled. It is a word to strengthen faith when circumstances seem contrary.

sens: a period of about thirty days, the twelfth part of the year
the duration of a lunar cycle, marked by the phases of the moon
an indeterminate but limited interval of time
new moon, lunar festival
G3376.detail:
1. The month is the fundamental calendar division: twelve months make a year. It is a regular and recognized measure of time. When Elizabeth remains pregnant and hides "for five months" (Luke 1:24), it is a precise and observable duration.

2. The Greek word comes from the moon (Greek "sélénè" = moon), as the ancients marked the months by the lunar phases. The new moon was celebrated as a feast (Galatians 4:10 places the months on the same level as religious festivals to observe).

3. Often, "month" also designates an intermediate period: Paul "stayed a year and six months" in Corinth (Acts 18:11), or the apostle "remained three months" in Malta (Acts 28:11). It is a convenient marker for counting time.
G3376.origine: The Greek word "mēn" is related to the moon and the word "mèniskos" (crescent). In Hebrew, "ḥodesh" (month) comes from a root meaning "new moon" or "renewal," as each month begins with a new moon. The biblical calendar was lunar, and the word "yareakh" (moon, rare in Greek) sometimes also designates the month. For the Greeks too, the month was a unit linked to the lunar cycle: hence this name relationship.
G3376.emploi: The word "month" appears 18 times in the provided New Testament verses, especially in Luke and Revelation. In Luke, it counts the months of pregnancy (Elizabeth, 1:24) or stays (Mary with Elizabeth, 1:56). In Acts, Paul or the travelers measure their journeys and residences in months (18:11, 28:11). Revelation uses it to mark durations of judgment: "forty-two months" (11:2), "five months" of torment (9:5), or "twelve months" of heavenly fruits (22:2). Galatians 4:10 mentions the worship of days and months, reproaching the Galatian converts for returning to Jewish observances.
G3376.portee: Understanding the notion of month helps the reader grasp time in the biblical narrative — the delays of pregnancy, journeys, durations of prophetic judgment. For Revelation, the symbolic months (42 months, 5 months) are not just numbers: they mark real or figurative periods of God's plan, inviting the believer to recognize that all times are in His hand.

sens: Reveal something hidden or unknown
Declare, announce publicly
Inform someone of a threat or danger
Warn someone to guard against something
G3377.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to reveal what was unknown or secret: Moses "made known" the resurrection of the dead by speaking of the burning bush, showing that this truth was hidden in the Scriptures and that he brings it to light (Luke 20:37).
2. In a legal or official context, the word means to declare, report to someone: the religious leaders ordered that if anyone discovered where Jesus was, they should "declare" it immediately, that is, report it (John 11:57).
3. The word takes on a more urgent meaning when it comes to warning of danger: the Roman tribune "informed" Paul of an ambush that awaited him and sent him to safety (Acts 23:30).
4. Finally, it can mean to warn to protect someone's conscience: the one who informs a Christian that meat comes from an idol sacrifice warns them against a moral peril (1 Corinthians 10:28).
G3377.origine: The Greek verb comes from a root that evokes the idea of pointing out, signaling. Its fundamental meaning is "to bring to light," "to make visible." The word is used in Greek documents to announce news, report a fact, and particularly to denounce or signal to an authority. It is an active verb that expresses the initiative of the speaker: it does not wait for someone to ask, it takes the initiative to reveal or warn.
G3377.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, in various contexts. In Luke 20:37, it is about declaring a theological truth drawn from Scripture. In John 11:57, it is used in a context of denunciation, the authorities seeking to arrest Jesus. In Acts 23:30, the tribune uses this verb to inform the governor of a threat against a prisoner. In 1 Corinthians 10:28, it designates the warning that someone gives to a believer to protect their conscience. The meaning nuances according to the context: theological revelation, denunciation, official report, or fraternal warning.
G3377.portee: This word reminds us that the truth about God and Christ had to be revealed, brought to light, and that it is transmitted by witnesses who speak of it. It also suggests that Christians have a responsibility to warn their brothers when they see them in danger, whether moral or spiritual, in a spirit of protection rather than condemnation.

sens: the part of the leg between the hip and the knee
the symbol of strength and power
G3382.detail:
1. The thigh is the part of the body that extends from the hip to the knee. It is one of the largest muscle masses in the human body. In Revelation 19:16, the resurrected and glorified Christ has written on his thigh the name "King of kings and Lord of lords" — a highly visible and prestigious place on the garment.
2. In the Bible, the thigh represents strength, power, and authority. This is why it is mentioned when one wants to emphasize dominion or majesty: here, the inscription on Christ's thigh affirms his absolute power over all creation.
G3382.origine: The Greek word μηρός comes from an Indo-European root designating the leg or limb. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament regularly translates יָרֵךְ (yarek) as μηρός. The thigh, as a part of the body associated with muscular strength, has taken on a symbolic charge in biblical cultures: to swear "by the thigh" of someone (Gen 24:2-3) was to swear by their power or authority.
G3382.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 19:16. John sees the victorious Christ clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and on this garment and on his thigh is engraved a name proclaiming his supreme royalty. This unique occurrence is highly symbolic: the mention of the thigh adds to the image of power and royal majesty.
G3382.portee: This word reminds us that the power of Christ is not hidden or mysterious: it is visibly inscribed on him, proclaimed unequivocally. Seeing the name of his dominion engraved on his thigh is to recognize that his victory is total, visible, indisputable. This invites the believer to accept the absolute authority of the risen Christ over their life.

sens: Particle that unites two successive negations: neither one nor the other
After a negative verb, it reinforces the negation by excluding several elements
In a prohibition, it sets a negative alternative
It excludes several things as a whole
G3383.detail:
1. This word connects two (or more) negations to say that none of these things exists or happens. It's like saying "not this AND not that" — both are excluded together. For example, in Acts 23:8, the Sadducees say that there exists "neither angel nor spirit": neither one nor the other.

2. When a sentence already begins with a negation ("ne"), the word "neither" adds other things to exclude. This is to avoid repeating "ne" in front of each term. Luke 7:33 speaks of John the Baptist: "not eating bread and not drinking wine" — in Greek, this is written with a single negation followed by "neither".

3. In commands or prohibitions, it sets negative alternatives: "do not swear either by heaven or by earth". This is less an affirmation than a prohibition that extends. Matthew 5:34 and 5:36 show this in Jesus' teaching on oaths.

4. Sometimes, the word excludes a single thing after an already negative sentence: "do not be shaken by any inspiration or any word" (2 Thessalonians 2:2) — the meaning is: "none of these things should trouble you."
G3383.origine: It is a negative particle composed of the root "mé-" (the non in Greek) and the suffix "-te" which connects two terms. It relates to Greek logic: while "non" opposes a fact ("it is" or "it is not"), the word "neither" excludes several things in a list. In Hebrew of the Old Testament, the equivalent is often repeated "lo" or "en", or the form "gam lo" ("neither... nor"). This particle is very Greek: it structures logical thought by denying step by step.
G3383.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the epistles. It serves to enumerate what does not exist, should not happen, or has not occurred. In Jesus' teachings (Matthew 5), it frames prohibitions on oaths by excluding several forms of swearing. In the Acts of the Apostles, it is found when reporting the beliefs of the Sadducees (Acts 23:8) or the plans of the conspirators (Acts 23:21). It also appears in pastoral warnings (2 Thessalonians 2:2) to exclude several sources of trouble. Each time, it constructs a negation that extends over several items: it is a tool for logical clarity.
G3383.portee: This word teaches the reader how the Bible states refusals and exclusions: not out of fear or doubt, but through clear logic that enumerates what should not be. When Jesus says "do not swear either by heaven or by earth", he constructs a refusal that applies to all possible false oaths. It is a total refusal, without escape. For the believer, it is a lesson: Christian truth firmly and systematically excludes certain things, not randomly.

sens: Woman who has given birth to a child
One who raises and nourishes the child
One who replaces the mother through affection and care
City or nation as a source and protector of its inhabitants
Symbolic figure of a power or spiritual reality
G3384.detail:
1. The mother is the pregnant woman and one who gives birth: Mary is called the "mother" of Jesus even before his birth (Matthew 1:18), and she brings him to life by carrying and nourishing him (Luke 7:15).
2. The mother is one who raises her child with tenderness and authority: she brings him to the temple (Luke 2:43), she searches for him with concern (Luke 2:48), and she treasures his words in her heart (Luke 2:51).
3. Jesus broadens the word "mother" to those who do the will of God with the same devotion: "Whoever does the will of my Father, he is my mother" (Matthew 12:50), and Paul calls Priscilla a "mother" for her affection towards her brothers (Romans 16:13).
4. A city or nation can be called "mother" as one who gives birth to and nourishes its inhabitants: the heavenly Jerusalem is "our mother" who gives birth to us for freedom (Galatians 4:26).
5. In a symbolic vision, Babylon is the "mother of harlots" (Revelation 17:5), meaning the source and queen of idolatries that corrupt the world.
G3384.origine: The Greek word mètēr comes from an ancient root that designates the biological and nurturing bond between a woman and her child. It is the same word found in all Indo-European languages (French "mère", Latin "mater", English "mother"). In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew "èm" (אֵם), which also carries the idea of source and origin. The word evokes the concrete image of one who carries and nourishes, and thereby engenders a relationship of affection and mutual recognition.
G3384.emploi: The word "mother" appears 78 times in the New Testament, mainly in the four Gospels and the Epistles. It primarily refers to the biological mother of Jesus, Mary, and the mothers of the disciples. It takes on a spiritual meaning when Jesus says that whoever does the will of God becomes his brother, sister, mother (Matthew 12:50, Mark 3:35): it is not about carnal generation, but the bond created by obedience and love. Paul treats Timothy with the affection of a "mother" (1 Timothy 5:2), while the new Jerusalem is called "our mother" as the heavenly city that gives birth to believers (Galatians 4:26). Finally, Babylon is symbolically described as the "mother of harlots" (Revelation 17:5), where the word expresses the evil origin and corrupting power.
G3384.portee: This word reminds believers that spiritual motherhood surpasses carnal motherhood: one who does the will of God is closer to the Lord than one who simply carries him in her womb. It invites recognition of the Church as a "mother" that nourishes us and gives us birth to divine life. It is also a call to filial respect towards our parents according to the commandment (Mark 7:10), reflecting the relationship of God's people towards the heavenly city from which they come.

sens: Interrogative particle expecting a negative response in a rhetorical question
Doubtful or perplexing question: wondering if something is possible
Direct question expressing an objection or surprise
Particle used to formulate an indirect question after verbs of knowledge or speech
G3385.detail:
1. This particle introduces a question posed in such a way that a "no" answer is expected. The speaker already knows the answer they desire and poses the question to make the listener reflect or to lead them to recognize an obvious truth. Example: "Do grapes gather from thorns?" (Matthew 7:16) — no one expects to gather grapes from thorns, so the question is rhetorical.
2. The particle can also express hesitation or perplexity in the face of something that seems suspicious or contrary to expectations. The one asking the question is genuinely hesitant but leans toward a negative answer. Example: "Can anyone forbid water, that these should not be baptized who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" (Acts 10:47) — Peter doubts, but logic leads him to lean toward refusing such a prohibition.
3. In a direct question, it expresses an objection, surprise, or doubt about what has just been heard. Example: "Is it I, Lord?" (Matthew 26:22) — the disciples are surprised and pained to hear that one of them will betray.
4. It can also serve in indirect questions, introducing a reported inquiry after a verb of speech or knowledge, where it remains an interrogative particle naturally expecting a negative response.
G3385.origine: The word μήτι is composed of μή, a particle of negation, and τι, the interrogative pronoun "who? what?" Its primary image is that of negation combined with questioning: it is a "negative question." In biblical Hebrew, it often corresponds to the particle ה (he interrogative) or אִם (im), which also pose questions expecting a negative response. This combination of negation and inquiry reflects the Semitic way of thinking, where asking a question in this manner implicitly suggests that there is no positive answer.
G3385.emploi: This particle appears about 18 times in the New Testament, almost always in the Gospels and Pauline epistles. It is primarily used in three contexts: first, rhetorical questions (Matthew 7:16, Mark 4:21) where an absurd thing is asked to implicitly deny it; second, questions of objection or surprise (Matthew 26:22, Mark 14:19) where the disciples are astonished or wonder if something serious is true; finally, questions expressing sincere perplexity or a request for permission (Acts 10:47). In all cases, the particle directs the interlocutor toward a negative response or invites reflection on the absurdity or incongruity of what is proposed.
G3385.portee: This particle shows how Jesus and the apostles teach: not through blunt assertions, but by asking questions that provoke thought and guide the heart toward truth. It also reveals how the Bible respects doubt and sincere inquiry, even in the face of holy matters. The use of μήτι invites the reader to become an active participant in the dialogue rather than a passive listener, making the teaching more vibrant and personal.

sens: Organ of the female body where the child develops during pregnancy
Capacity to conceive and give life
Source or origin from which something proceeds
G3388.detail:
1. The word physiologically refers to the female organ where the child forms and grows before birth. In Romans 4:19, Paul mentions Sarah, who is no longer able to bear children: her womb, aged, can no longer conceive. This is the most direct and bodily sense.

2. By extension, the word evokes the vital power of generation, the capacity to conceive. When the law of Moses commands that "every male who opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord" (Luke 2:23), it speaks of the one who opened the womb, that is, the firstborn son from the mother's belly — the first fruit of fertility.

3. Figuratively, womb means that which generates, from which something proceeds, like a source or origin. The image of the generating belly extends to everything that produces or gives birth.
G3388.origine: The Greek word μήτρα (mētra) comes from an ancient root meaning "mother" — we find in French the word "mère" itself, and also "métropole" (mother city). In Hebrew, the corresponding word is רֶחֶם (reḥem), which means both "womb" and "mercy": the latter meaning comes from the idea that the womb is the place of maternal tenderness. The Greek primarily follows the bodily sense.
G3388.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament. In Luke 2:23, it appears in a citation of the Law that speaks of the firstborn "who opens the womb" — this is a biblical Hebrewism for saying the firstborn. In Romans 4:19, Paul uses it in the literal sense: he describes the advanced age of Sarah, whose womb was dead, meaning sterile and unable to conceive. In both cases, the physiological sense dominates, but with a theological charge: the life that is born is a gift from God.
G3388.portee: This word reminds us that human life is born from the mother's womb and depends on God's creative power. In Romans 4:19, Sarah's sterility becomes a sign of human impossibility — and thus of the wonder of the miracle, since God will still give her a child. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize that all life comes from God and that His power surpasses our limits.

sens: One who kills his mother
By extension, one who strikes or injures his mother
G3389.detail:
1. The primary meaning is one who kills his mother — a grave crime known as matricide. It is an act of extreme violence against the parent who gave life. Paul lists it in 1 Timothy 1:9 among the sinners for whom the Law was given, alongside parricides (killers of fathers) and other criminals.
2. The word can also more broadly refer to one who strikes or injures his mother, even without lethal intent. This is suggested by the reference to Exodus 21:15, where Mosaic Law punished one who strikes his father or mother — a crime against parental honor and authority.
G3389.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: "mother" (μήτηρ) and "to strike" or "to injure" (ἀλοάω). It is a compound that paints the image of violence done to the one who bore us. In Hebrew, the concept is found in the laws regarding one who "strikes" his father or mother (Exodus 21:15), serious violations of the commandment to honor father and mother.
G3389.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 1:9. Paul uses it to enumerate the categories of sinners to whom the Mosaic Law addresses — those who commit serious crimes against the person and family. It appears in a list intended to show that the Law reveals sin in its most obvious and repugnant forms. This context underscores the absolute gravity of the crime: striking or killing one's own mother violates not only the law but also the nature and respect due to parents.
G3389.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of the depth of evil that sin can produce — even the most sacred relationship, that between mother and child, can be corrupted by sin. Paul cites this extreme crime to show that God's Law states what is right and unequivocally condemns acts that are most contrary to the created order. It is also a call to take seriously the commandment to honor father and mother, not only in words but in actions.

sens: To make impure or dirty in a physical sense, in the rules of ritual purity
To soil or stain morality, conscience, personal purity
To profane or violate what is holy
G3392.detail:
1. In the context of the Mosaic law, to defile means to contract a ritual impurity that prevents the performance of certain religious acts: the Jews do not want to enter the praetorium with Pilate for fear of becoming defiled and thus being unable to eat the Passover (John 18:28). It is primarily a matter of conformity to the rules of worship.

2. To defile can also describe a moral corruption, when a person's soul or conscience becomes impure through sin or unbelief: Titus 1:15 states that for those who are defiled and unbelieving, even pure things do not remain pure, for their minds and consciences are defiled. The word then denotes how sin stains the inner person.

3. Finally, to defile can mean to profane or violate what is sacred through carnal or depraved acts: in Jude 1:8, false teachers defile their flesh by engaging in immorality, which constitutes a contempt for divine order.
G3392.origine: The Greek word miainô comes from a root that evokes the idea of soiling or staining. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew tamé (טָמֵא), which means to be impure or contaminated in both ritual and moral senses. The word family includes expressions related to purity and impurity, which are fundamental in the law of Moses.
G3392.emploi: The verb to defile appears four times in the New Testament, in very varied contexts. In John 18:28, it concerns ritual impurity in the strict sense, according to Jewish law. In Titus 1:15, it describes the moral defilement that results from unbelief and sin, which affects the conscience of the one who is affected. In Hebrews 12:15, it denotes how trouble or bitterness can contaminate an entire community. In Jude 1:8, it applies to carnal corruption and contempt for divine authority. The word thus oscillates between legal impurity, moral corruption, and profanation of the sacred.
G3392.portee: This word reminds the Christian that sin is not merely a legal or external issue: it defiles the soul, the conscience, and wounds our communion with God. Understanding defilement helps to grasp why Jesus emphasizes inner purity and why God's grace purifies us deeply. It is a call to watch over the sanctification of our hearts and actions.

sens: Moral or spiritual dirt that makes impure
Corruption or moral degradation
G3393.detail:
1. Defilement is a spiritual contamination, a moral impurity that attaches to the soul like a stain. It is the state of one who has allowed themselves to be affected by evil or sin. In 2 Peter 2:20, Peter speaks of the "defilements of the world" — everything that corrupts and degrades morally those who turn away from Christ.
2. The word also evokes progressive degradation: a person who turns away from the right path defiles themselves through their bad choices, and this defilement accumulates like a buildup of dirt. That is why Peter says that the last condition of one who falls back is "worse than the first" — the defilement has worsened.
G3393.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb miainô, which means "to defile" or "to contaminate." It is a very concrete image: that of something pure becoming dirty, stained. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates Hebrew words that denote abomination or filth (שִׁקּוּץ, "that which is repugnant"). The word family emphasizes the idea of stain or pollution that attaches.
G3393.emploi: This word appears only once in 2 Peter 2:20, in the plural ("defilements"). Peter uses it to refer to the moral and spiritual corruptions of the world — sins, immoral pleasures, false doctrines — from which Christians are supposed to have turned away through conversion. The context speaks of renegades who, knowing Christ, voluntarily plunge back into evil: they submit again to the defilements. It is a rare, grave word that underscores the moral horror of apostasy.
G3393.portee: This word highlights the reality of sin: it is not merely a violation of a rule, but a true contamination that defiles the soul. For a Christian, it reminds us that conversion has separated us from the defilements of the world, and that returning to sin is never neutral — it is to soil oneself again. Peter warns us that this relapse makes the state worse than before, for one who knows Christ and renounces Him covers themselves with an even graver defilement.

sens: Moral or spiritual defilement
Corruption of carnal desire
Contempt for the order established by God
G3394.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a defilement, a stain that soils — not only physically, but morally and spiritually. It is the state of one who has allowed themselves to be corrupted. In 2 Peter 2:10, the apostle speaks of those who follow carnal desires in a quest for impurity: they are internally defiled by their disordered passions.
2. Impurity is expressed here in the flesh, that is, in carnal desires that rebel against the will of God. It is not merely an action, but a state of corruption of the heart that drives to action.
3. This impurity is accompanied by contempt for authority (in 2 Peter 2:10, the same verse speaks of those who despise the authority of angels and magistrates). It reflects a desire to free oneself from all moral and spiritual restraint, a distancing from the fear of God.
G3394.origine: The word comes from the verb "miainô" (μιαίνω), which means "to defile, to contaminate." It shares this root with "miasma" (μίασμα), a term that literally evokes a stain or pollution. The basic notion is that of a defilement that adheres and corrupts whatever it touches — like a stain that does not wash away. In Hebrew, words like "tumah" express a similar idea: ritual and moral impurity that separates from God.
G3394.emploi: The word appears only once in the preserved New Testament: in 2 Peter 2:10. Peter uses it to condemn false teachers who are dominated by the desires of the flesh. Impurity there is not a mere passing sin, but a direction of the heart: these men "follow after the flesh in a desire for impurity." It goes hand in hand with arrogance and contempt for authority. It is a picture of the total corruption of a person, both internally and in their behavior.
G3394.portee: This word warns the believer that impurity is not a private matter or without consequence. It corrupts the one who surrenders to it and removes the fear of God from them. It leads to contempt for the order that God has established. The choice to follow Christ means turning away from this defilement and seeking the purity of heart, which comes from obedience to God.

sens: A mixture of substances, a combination of distinct products
A preparation composed, especially of spices or perfumes
G3395.detail:
1. A mixture refers to the combination of several different substances brought together. In John 19:39, Nicodemus brings a mixture of myrrh and aloes: two precious resins mixed together, probably powdered, to embalm the body of Jesus after His death. It is a fragrant and preservative compound.

2. More broadly, the word denotes a preparation, a mixture, particularly in the realm of aromatic or medicinal substances. The image is that of various ingredients intentionally combined to achieve a specific effect.
G3395.origine: The word comes from the verb "mignymi" (μίγνυμι) which means "to mix." It is derived from the Greek root concerning the action of joining, combining distinct elements. The word is relatively rare in ancient texts; it appears notably in cooking or pharmacy texts where ingredients are mixed.
G3395.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 19:39. It describes the mixture of myrrh and aloes that Nicodemus brings for the burial of Jesus. It is a specialized term used to evoke a carefully composed preparation, appropriate for an act of honor and devotion towards the deceased according to Jewish customs.
G3395.portee: This mixture symbolizes the honor rendered to Jesus in His death: Nicodemus, who had visited Him secretly at night, finally shows himself openly and generously to bury Him. The hundred pounds of this costly mixture manifest the respect and love of the disciple for his master. It is an act of faith performed without fear, at the moment of the Passion.

sens: Combine two or more substances together
Join different elements in a mixture
Unite intimately two distinct things
G3396.detail: 1. Mix means to combine two or more substances to form a whole where they are intimately united. It refers to the concrete mixing of liquids or physical elements: Matthew 27:34 describes the wine "mixed" with gall, where gall is poured into the wine to make it bitter. 2. The word is used for situations where very different realities are united together, often in a disturbing or dark way. In Revelation 8:7, hail and fire are "mixed" with blood: the image is of three elements that merge in a horrific manner. 3. Similarly, in Luke 13:1, the blood of the Galileans is "mixed" with that of their sacrifices: two realities—murder and worship—are violently confused. 4. In Revelation 15:2, a sea of glass is "mixed" with fire: the peaceful and luminous heavenly atmosphere also contains the fire of judgment. Everywhere, the verb creates the idea of a fusion where elements retain their identity but are united, often with a tone of contrast or tension.
G3396.origine: The verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of joining, pouring together. In classical Greek, mignumi is used for all types of mixtures: pouring wine and water, mixing colors or flavors. The word is close to the verb kerannyumi (to mix, to dip), which shares a similar nuance. In the Greek Old Testament, the verb translates the Hebrew arav, which also carries the idea of mixing or intertwining.
G3396.emploi: The verb mignumi appears four times in the Segond, always in the New Testament. In Matthew 27:34, it describes the wine offered to Jesus at the cross, mixed with gall—a mixture intended to dull the suffering but remains bitter. In Luke 13:1, Jesus hears about Galileans whose blood was mixed with the sacrifices: the profanation of worship is expressed by this forced mixture. In Revelation 8:7 and 15:2, the verb appears in two heavenly visions: hail and fire mixed with blood during judgment, then the sea of glass mixed with fire in the heavenly court. Each usage emphasizes the unusual union of two realities: the bitterness of the passion, the horror of murder during worship, the judgment of heaven upon the earth, and divine holiness tinged with justice.
G3396.portee: This verb helps us understand how the Bible can describe complex realities where good and evil, grace and judgment, intersect. At the cross, the mixed wine symbolizes the bitterness that Jesus accepted. In the visions of Revelation, the unusual mixtures remind us that the kingdom of God brings judgment: the fire of judgment mingles with images of heavenly peace. This word invites the believer to see that God's will can unite realities that seem opposed, and that this union often has a profound meaning.

sens: Of reduced size, of small dimension
Scarce, few in number
Short-lived
Of little importance, of lower rank or influence
Young, not yet grown up
G3398.detail:
1. Small literally means of small size or of low physical dimension. Zacchaeus was of small stature (Luke 19:3), and a mustard seed is the smallest of all seeds (Matthew 13:32).

2. Small can also refer to a reduced quantity: a little leaven is enough to leaven the whole dough (1 Corinthians 5:6), and a church may have little power but faithfully keep the word of God (Revelation 3:8).

3. Small also describes what lasts a short time: "A little while longer, and the world will see me no more" (John 14:19), or "shortly thereafter" (Matthew 26:73).

4. Small can express a lack of importance or rank: whoever humbles himself the most among the disciples is the greatest in the eyes of Jesus (Luke 9:48), and little children have a special place in the kingdom of God (Matthew 18:6, 10).

5. Small designates what is young or a child: receiving a little child in the name of Christ is to receive Christ himself (Luke 9:48).
G3398.origine: The Greek word mikros comes from an Indo-European root that denotes the small, the reduced, the fragmented. In ancient Greek, it contrasts with megas (large) and describes anything that does not reach the normal or expected dimension. In the Greek Old Testament, it generally translates the Hebrew qatan (קָטָן), which has the same concrete and figurative meaning. The word is used in the literal sense (size), then by extension in the figurative sense (importance, authority, duration).
G3398.emploi: Mikros appears 43 times in the New Testament. It first applies to physical dimensions: people (Zacchaeus, the child Jesus), seeds, objects. Very often, it takes on a figurative sense of importance or rank: the "little ones" in Matthew 18 refer to humble disciples or children, deemed important in the kingdom despite their apparent insignificance. The word also qualifies what is scarce (leaven, power), and what is brief in time ("a little while"). John frequently uses this temporal sense: "A little while longer" recurs several times in Jesus' farewell discourses (John 13-16). Luke and Matthew use it to mark the humility or apparent weakness of the disciples and churches.
G3398.portee: This word invites the believer to reverse the values of the world. What seems small, insignificant, powerless—a child, a humble disciple, a weak church—is of great dignity in the eyes of Jesus. It also reminds us that Christ's time on earth is short, and that every moment counts. Finally, smallness is not an excuse: a little leaven leavens the whole lump, so even the smallest moral failing has consequences.

sens: Port city on the Aegean coast, in the region of Caria (Asia Minor)
G3399.detail: Miletus is an important maritime city of ancient Asia Minor, located on the coast of Caria. It is a strategic port on the eastern Mediterranean where Paul stops during his missionary journeys.
G3399.origine: Miletus is an ancient Greek colony, founded by Ionians. Its Greek name Milêtos designates this port city. It was one of the largest Greek cities in Asia Minor, renowned for its maritime trade and cultural role.
G3399.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in relation to the apostle Paul. In Acts 20:15, Paul arrives at Miletus during his journey to Jerusalem. In Acts 20:17, Paul sends to Miletus for the elders of the Church of Ephesus to say his farewells: it is at Miletus that Paul delivers his final address to the leaders of the Church in Asia. In 2 Timothy 4:20, Paul mentions that he left his companion Trophimus sick at Miletus, which shows that Paul must have passed through this region again during later travels.
